cmo-cmo-1995-01.title: Pair x with 1 - x
cmo-cmo-1995-01.body:
For every real $x$,
$$f(1 - x) = \frac{9^{1-x}}{9^{1-x} + 3} = \frac{9}{9 + 3\cdot 9^x} = \frac{3}{9^x + 3}$$
(multiply numerator and denominator by $9^x$), so
$$f(x) + f(1 - x) = \frac{9^x + 3}{9^x + 3} = 1.$$
Pair the term $k$ with the term $1996 - k$ for $k = 1, \ldots, 997$: these $997$ pairs contribute $1$ each. The only unpaired term is $k = 998$, i.e. $f\left(\frac12\right) = \frac{3}{3 + 3} = \frac12$. Therefore the sum is
$$997 + \frac12 = \frac{1995}{2}.$$
(Numerical check: summing the $1995$ terms directly gives $997.5$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{1995}{2} = 997\tfrac12$** ∎

cmo-cmo-1995-02.title: Cube and regroup
cmo-cmo-1995-02.body:
Both sides are positive, so it is equivalent to prove $a^{3a}b^{3b}c^{3c} \ge (abc)^{a+b+c}$. Now
$$\frac{a^{3a}b^{3b}c^{3c}}{(abc)^{a+b+c}} = a^{2a - b - c}\, b^{2b - a - c}\, c^{2c - a - b} = \left(\frac ab\right)^{a-b}\left(\frac bc\right)^{b-c}\left(\frac ac\right)^{a-c},$$
which one checks by comparing exponents: $a$ appears with exponent $(a - b) + (a - c) = 2a - b - c$, $b$ with $-(a - b) + (b - c) = 2b - a - c$, and $c$ with $-(b - c) - (a - c) = 2c - a - b$.

Each factor has the form $\left(\frac xy\right)^{x - y}$ with $x, y > 0$, and such a factor is $\ge 1$: if $x \ge y$ then the base is $\ge 1$ and the exponent $\ge 0$; if $x < y$ then the base is $< 1$ and the exponent $< 0$. Hence the product is $\ge 1$, which proves the inequality (with equality iff $a = b = c$). ∎

cmo-cmo-1995-02.title: Weighted means
cmo-cmo-1995-02.body:
Consider the numbers $a, b, c$ with weights $a, b, c$. The weighted geometric mean is at least the weighted harmonic mean, and the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean, so
$$\left(a^a b^b c^c\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b+c}} \ge \frac{a + b + c}{\frac aa + \frac bb + \frac cc} = \frac{a + b + c}{3} \ge \sqrt[3]{abc}.$$
Raising to the power $a + b + c > 0$ gives $a^a b^b c^c \ge (abc)^{\frac{a+b+c}{3}}$. ∎

(Equivalently, taking logarithms: the inequality says $\sum a\ln a \ge \frac{a+b+c}{3}\sum\ln a$, i.e. $\sum_{\text{pairs}} (a - b)(\ln a - \ln b) \ge 0$ after multiplying by $3$, and each term is $\ge 0$ because $\ln$ is increasing.)

cmo-cmo-1995-03.title: Count angles
cmo-cmo-1995-03.body:
Call the interior angle greater than $180^\circ$ of a boomerang its *reflex angle*, and its vertex the *reflex vertex*. Every quadrilateral here is simple (its sides do not cross), so its interior angles add up to $2\pi$, and the total of all interior angles of the $q$ quadrilaterals is $2\pi q$.

**Angles at the vertices of $C$.** Let $X$ be a vertex of $C$; its angle in $C$ is less than $\pi$. Near $X$, the region $C$ is a sector of angle less than $\pi$; a quadrilateral containing $X$ in the interior of one of its sides would cover a half-disc around $X$, and one containing $X$ in its interior a full disc, both impossible. So every quadrilateral containing $X$ has $X$ as a vertex, and since the quadrilaterals tile $C$ without overlapping, their angles at $X$ add up to the angle of $C$ at $X$. Summing over the $s$ vertices, these angles total $(s - 2)\pi$.

**Angles at the reflex vertices.** Let $R$ be the reflex vertex of a boomerang $Q_0$. $R$ cannot lie on the boundary of $C$: near a boundary point, $C$ occupies an angle of at most $\pi$, while $Q_0$ alone occupies an angle greater than $\pi$ there. So $R$ is an interior point of $C$, and the quadrilaterals cover a full neighbourhood of $R$. Another quadrilateral containing $R$ on the interior of a side would occupy an angle $\pi$ at $R$, and $\pi + (\text{reflex angle}) > 2\pi$, impossible without overlapping; so all quadrilaterals containing $R$ have $R$ as a vertex and their angles at $R$ add up to exactly $2\pi$. In particular no other boomerang has its reflex vertex at $R$ (two reflex angles would exceed $2\pi$), so the $b$ reflex vertices are distinct points, all different from the vertices of $C$.

**Conclusion.** The angles counted at the vertices of $C$ and at the $b$ reflex vertices are different angles of the quadrilaterals, so
$$2\pi q \ge (s - 2)\pi + 2\pi b, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad q \ge b + \frac{s - 2}{2}.$$ ∎

cmo-cmo-1995-04.title: Equal terms
cmo-cmo-1995-04.body:
Let $q$ be any positive integer and put
$$x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n = n^{2k+1}q^{3k+2}, \qquad y = n^2q^3.$$
Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^3 = n\cdot n^{6k+3}q^{9k+6} = n^{6k+4}q^{9k+6} = \left(n^2q^3\right)^{3k+2} = y^{3k+2}.$$
Different $q$ give different $y$, so this is an infinite family of solutions in positive integers. ∎

cmo-cmo-1995-04.title: Sum of cubes
cmo-cmo-1995-04.body:
Since $1^3 + 2^3 + \cdots + n^3 = c^2$ with $c = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, for every positive integer $q$
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\left(i\,c^kq^{3k+2}\right)^3 = c^{3k}q^{3(3k+2)}\cdot c^2 = c^{3k+2}q^{3(3k+2)} = (cq^3)^{3k+2}.$$
So $x_i = i\,c^kq^{3k+2}$, $y = cq^3$ ($q = 1, 2, \ldots$) are infinitely many solutions. (For $k = 0$ and $q = 1$ this is just $1^3 + \cdots + n^3 = c^2$.) ∎

cmo-cmo-1995-05.title: The sequence decreases by at least u
cmo-cmo-1995-05.body:
**$f$ maps $[0, 1]$ to $[0, 1]$.** (The two formulas agree at $x = u$, where the second gives $1 - (u + 1 - u)^2 = 0$.) For $u \le x \le 1$, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
$$\sqrt{ux} + \sqrt{(1-u)(1-x)} \le \sqrt{(u + 1 - u)(x + 1 - x)} = 1,$$
so $0 \le f(x) \le 1$. Hence the sequence is well defined and stays in $[0, 1]$.

**Key estimate: $f(x) \le x - u$ for $u \le x \le 1$.** Expanding,
$$f(x) = 1 - ux - (1-u)(1-x) - 2\sqrt{ux(1-u)(1-x)} = u + x - 2ux - 2\sqrt{ux(1-u)(1-x)}.$$
Since $x \ge u$ and $1 - u \ge 1 - x \ge 0$, we have $ux(1-u)(1-x) \ge u\cdot u\cdot(1-x)(1-x)$, so $\sqrt{ux(1-u)(1-x)} \ge u(1-x)$ and
$$f(x) \le u + x - 2ux - 2u(1 - x) = x - u.$$

**Conclusion.** $u_1 = f(1) = 1 - u$. As long as $u_1, \ldots, u_n$ are all $> u$, the estimate gives $u_{i+1} \le u_i - u$, so
$$0 \le u_{n+1} \le u_1 - nu = 1 - (n+1)u.$$
This is impossible for $n + 1 > \frac1u$, so some term $u_j$ satisfies $0 \le u_j \le u$, and then $u_{j+1} = f(u_j) = 0$. So $k = j + 1$ works. ∎
